source_title: Oracle's debt is growing. The tech giant's investors are concerned
source_excerpt:
Embed Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6007863/nx-s1-9973859" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Oracle, the multinational tech giant has taken on a lot of loans to build up its AI capacity. But Oracle's investors are not happy with this piling debt load.
LEILA FADEL, HOST: Tech giant Oracle has added a lot of debt lately, which is drawing questions from Wall Street investors. Our colleagues Rick Mulvey and Adrian Ma at The Indicator explain how Oracle's fortunes and the AI boom connect to the wider economy. ADRIAN MA, BYLINE: Oracle is one of those companies that you've probably heard of but may not deal with directly. It's a multinational tech giant that sells enterprise software and computing power. RICKY MULVEY, BYLINE: Yeah. The vast majority of big companies use its databases and software. MA: And about a decade ago, credit analysts viewed Oracle bonds as a safe investment. MATT SHERIDAN: They were a high-margin software company. Now they're a capital-intensive data center buildout? This was a huge shift. MA: Matt Sheridan is a senior lecturer in the finance department at... SHERIDAN: The Ohio State University. MULVEY: Matt analyzed credit before working as a professor too. SHERIDAN: The biggest issue with Oracle is that load has nearly doubled in the last two years. They're sitting at 169 billion in total debt. MA: Oracle went into the AI boom in a weaker financial spot than other tech giants. MULVEY: Larry Ellison is the co-founder, executive chairman at Oracle. He thinks that training AI models is a huge business opportunity. MA: So why aren't Oracle investors happy? MULVEY: One reason is the sheer size of the debt. It's turned Oracle from a business that generates cash into one that burns money. MA: Another is that the path back to profitability may take some time. Building data centers takes a second. MULVEY: Oracle is relying on OpenAI a lot. Sam Altman and the folks at OpenAI promised Oracle they would pay about $300 billion over the next five or so years. Oracle's data centers help power ChatGPT. MA: And OpenAI's financials come with a lot of open questions, mostly because you probably can't see them. MULVEY: And Matt says if OpenAI's financials were out in the open, its value would also be based on its actual numbers. SHERIDAN: So if you can't really trust that OpenAI's revenues are going to be growing at parabolic speed, that trickles into Oracle. MA: Oracle and OpenAI are not just in a customer-seller relationship. This bit has more implications for the wider economy. MULVEY: OpenAI pays Oracle to use its cloud infrastructure and says it'll pay a lot more in the coming years. So Oracle buys chips from Nvidia to build this cloud even more. And then Nvidia invests money into OpenAI so that OpenAI can buy computing space from Oracle, which, remember, is buying those Nvidia chips. MA: I'm just picturing a circle. And according to credit investors, Oracle is a weak link in this circular economy. MULVEY: Oracle has already signaled that it may run into trouble paying back its loans on time. This notice created some alarming headlines, but Matt says it actually could benefit Oracle. It allows the company to delay payments, though it's still on the hook for the full amount. MA: Still, Oracle's credit investors are pricing in more risk. S&P, the big credit rating agency - they downgraded Oracle's credit in July. Now Oracle is barely above junk status. Matt says these circular deals and heavy amounts of debt could lead to real problems for the economy as a whole. SHERIDAN: And that makes me concerned that if this is a bubble, it's going to be more like a Lehman Brothers-type event. And they're all becoming very interconnected. MA: For now, the wheel is still turning. MULVEY: Ricky Mulvey. MA: Adrian Ma, NPR News. (SOUNDBITE OF POLYPHIA'S "G.O.A.T.") Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
